lead: Parallel resonance happens when the capacitive and inductive susceptances in a parallel network are equal and opposite. They cancel, the tank looks purely resistive, and its impedance reaches a maximum. The supply then delivers minimum current, while the coil and capacitor exchange a much larger current between themselves. This idea sits inside every tuned radio stage, oscillator tank and filter that must pass one band and reject the rest. A real tank, a coil with resistance across a capacitor, is a series-parallel circuit with its own formulas.
prereq: You need: the resonance condition and Q from series resonance, and admittance of parallel AC branches.

sections.h3: Ideal parallel RLC: admittance does the work

blocks.text: Connect R, L and C in parallel across one AC source. All three carry the same voltage V, so currents add and admittances add. The input admittance is:
Here y is admittance in siemens (S), R is resistance in ohms (Ω), L is inductance in henries (H), C is capacitance in farads (F), and ω = 2πf is angular frequency in rad/s.
At resonance the imaginary part is zero: ω₀C = 1/(ω₀L). This gives the same resonant frequency as the series case:
Here ω₀ is resonant angular frequency in rad/s; f₀ is resonant frequency in Hz; L is inductance in H; C is capacitance in F.

Now Y = 1/R, which is real. The impedance is Z = R and is maximum; the supply current I<sub>s</sub> = V/R is minimum. At lower f the term 1/(ωL) dominates and the tank looks inductive. At higher f the term ωC dominates and it looks capacitive.
The parallel quality factor is:
Q = R/(ω₀L) = ω₀CR = R√(C/L)
Here q is dimensionless; R is parallel resistance in Ω; ω₀ is in rad/s; L is in H; C is in F.

At f₀ the branch currents are I<sub>L</sub> = V/(ω₀L) and I<sub>C</sub> = Vω₀C. Their magnitudes equal Q I<sub>s</sub> and their phasors are opposite, so they cancel in the supply line. This is current magnification.

sections.h3: Practical tank: coil resistance shifts f₀

blocks.text: A real inductor is a coil with resistance r in series with L. Connect C across the coil. The coil branch has admittance:
Ycoil = 1/(r + jωL) = (r − jωL)/(r² + ω²L²)
Here r is coil resistance in Ω; L is coil inductance in H; ω is angular frequency in rad/s; j is the imaginary unit.
Add jωC. Resonance occurs when the total imaginary part is zero:
ωC = ωL/(r² + ω²L²)
Here ω is angular frequency in rad/s; C is capacitance in F; r is coil resistance in Ω; L is inductance in H.
Solving for ω gives the resonant frequency of the practical tank, the frequency at which the tank has unity power factor:
Here f₀ is resonant frequency in Hz; r is coil resistance in Ω; L is inductance in H; C is capacitance in F.

At this frequency the input impedance is resistive. Its value, the dynamic resistance, is R<sub>D</sub> = L/(rC). With the coil quality factor Q = ω₀L/r this is the same as R<sub>D</sub> = r(1 + Q²), about Q²r. A small r gives a large R<sub>D</sub> and a small supply current. The circuit is called a rejector or current-resonant tank: it rejects current from the source while a large current circulates in the coil and capacitor.

The coil resistance pulls f₀ below 1/(2π√(LC)); for r much smaller than ω₀L the shift is tiny and the ideal formula is close enough. If 1/(LC) ≤ (r/L)², the formula has no real solution: the tank never reaches unity power factor.
If the capacitor branch also has a resistance R<sub>C</sub> in series with C, set the total susceptance to zero in the same way. The result is the general series-parallel resonance condition:
ω₀ = (1/√(LC)) √[(r² − L/C)/(RC² − L/C)]

Here r is the coil resistance and R<sub>C</sub> the capacitor-branch resistance, in Ω. With R<sub>C</sub> = 0 it reduces to the practical-tank formula; if r = R<sub>C</sub> = √(L/C) the tank is resistive at every frequency.

items: Convert the source to a phasor and write each branch as an admittance.
Add the admittances and set the imaginary part to zero to find ω₀ or f₀.
Put ω₀ back into Y. The remaining real part gives Z at resonance; I<sub>s</sub> = V/Z.
Find coil and capacitor currents separately. At resonance they are nearly equal and opposite, each about Q times I<sub>s</sub>, with Q = ω₀L/r for a real coil.

blocks.text: The figure plots |Z| of the first worked example against frequency. The peak of 1 kΩ sits at f₀ = 1591.5 Hz, and the impedance falls to 707 Ω at the half-power points, 159 Hz apart. The right half shows the branch currents of the practical tank in the second example. The chapter on Q and bandwidth turns this sharpness into numbers.

items: At f₀ the tank power factor is unity because Y is real. The source sees R or R<sub>D</sub>.
A meter in the supply line reads the small current; a meter in the coil branch reads the large circulating current.

figure.caption: Left: the impedance of the ideal tank of the first example (R = 1 kΩ, L = 10 mH, C = 1 µF) peaks at 1 kΩ at f₀ and falls to 707 Ω at the half-power points, 159 Hz apart. Right: in the practical tank of the second example the coil and capacitor currents of about 100 mA nearly cancel, leaving 10 mA from the supply in phase with V.

spec.aria: Impedance magnitude of a parallel RLC tank against frequency peaking at 1 kilo-ohm, and a phasor diagram with the capacitor current 99.5 milliamps leading, the coil current 100 milliamps lagging 84 degrees, and the supply current 10 milliamps in phase.

examples.question: A parallel RLC circuit has R = 1 kΩ, L = 10 mH and C = 1 µF. A 10 V rms source drives it. Find f₀, Q, the bandwidth, the supply current at resonance and the circulating inductor current at resonance.
steps: At resonance Z = R = 1 kΩ, so I<sub>s</sub> = 10/1000 = 0.01 A = 10 mA.
examples.answer: f₀ = 1591.55 Hz, Q = 10, bandwidth = 159.15 Hz, supply current = 10 mA, and circulating current = 100 mA rms.
examples.check:
import math
R = 1000.0
L = 10e-3
C = 1e-6
V = 10.0
omega0 = 1/math.sqrt(L*C)
f0 = omega0/(2*math.pi)
Q = R/(omega0*L)
bw = f0/Q
Is = V/R
IL = V/(omega0*L)
IC = V*omega0*C
print(round(f0, 2))
print(round(Q, 2))
print(round(bw, 2))
print(round(Is*1000, 2))
print(round(IL*1000, 2))

examples.question: A coil of resistance 10 Ω and inductance 10 mH is connected in parallel with a 1 µF capacitor across a 10 V rms variable-frequency supply. Find the resonant frequency, the dynamic resistance, the supply current, the coil current and the capacitor current at resonance.
steps: Data: r = 10 Ω, L = 10 mH = 0.01 H, C = 1 µF = 10⁻⁶ F, V = 10 V rms.
ω₀ = √(10⁸ − 10⁶) = √(9.9 × 10⁷) = 9949.9 rad/s, so f₀ = 9949.9/(2π) = 1583.6 Hz, a little below the ideal 1591.5 Hz.
Supply current: I<sub>s</sub> = V/R<sub>D</sub> = 10/1000 = 10 mA, in phase with V.
Coil impedance at ω₀: ω₀L = 99.50 Ω, |Z<sub>coil</sub>| = √(10² + 99.50²) = 100.0 Ω, so I<sub>coil</sub> = 10/100 = 0.100 A, lagging V by arctan(99.50/10) = 84.3°.
Capacitor current: I<sub>C</sub> = Vω₀C = 10 × 9949.9 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.0995 A, leading V by 90°.

Check: the in-phase part of I<sub>coil</sub> is 0.100 × cos 84.3° = 0.0100 A = I<sub>s</sub>, and its reactive part 0.100 × sin 84.3° = 0.0995 A cancels I<sub>C</sub>. Q = ω₀L/r = 9.95 ≈ I<sub>C</sub>/I<sub>s</sub>.
examples.answer: f₀ ≈ 1583.6 Hz, R<sub>D</sub> = 1 kΩ, I<sub>s</sub> = 10 mA, I<sub>coil</sub> = 100 mA and I<sub>C</sub> = 99.5 mA.

traps: Impedance is maximum at parallel resonance, not minimum. Series resonance gives minimum impedance and maximum supply current.
At resonance the supply current is small, but the coil and capacitor currents are large and opposite. Do not assume branch current is zero.

Parallel Q has R in the numerator: Q = R/(ω₀L). Do not invert the series formula blindly; the two use different resistances (the shunt R of an ideal tank, the series r of a real coil, where Q = ω₀L/r).
A real coil's resistance lowers f₀ below 1/(2π√(LC)) and gives a finite dynamic resistance R<sub>D</sub> = L/(rC); the ideal formula can fail when r is large.

quiz.q: State the condition for resonance in an ideal parallel RLC circuit.
quiz.a: The susceptances cancel: ωC = 1/(ωL), so ω₀ = 1/√(LC).

quiz.q: Why can the supply current be minimum while the inductor current is large?
quiz.a: At resonance I<sub>L</sub> and I<sub>C</sub> are equal in magnitude and opposite in phase, so their sum in the supply line is small; each can be Q times I<sub>s</sub>.

quiz.q: An ideal parallel tank has R = 2 kΩ, L = 2 mH and C = 0.05 µF. Find f₀ and Q.
A practical coil tank is found to resonate below 1/(2π√(LC)). What causes this?
quiz.a: Coil resistance r in series with L changes the resonance condition; f₀ = (1/(2π))√(1/(LC) − (r/L)²).

quiz.q: At resonance in the first worked example the supply current is 10 mA and the inductor current is 100 mA. What is Q, and what is the phase relation between the inductor current and the capacitor current?
quiz.a: Q = I<sub>L</sub>/I<sub>s</sub> = 100/10 = 10. I<sub>L</sub> lags V by 90° and I<sub>C</sub> leads V by 90°, so they are equal in size and 180° apart; their sum is zero and only the 10 mA through R comes from the supply.

beyond: Not for the exam. Practical radio receivers use a coil-and-capacitor tank as the load of an RF amplifier, where the dynamic resistance sets gain and the loaded Q sets selectivity. Oscillator design uses the same tank, and phase noise depends on how strongly the active device loads it. Modern filter design replaces hand calculations with network synthesis and CAD, but the parallel-resonance idea remains the starting point. Search next for 'dynamic resistance of a parallel resonant circuit', 'loaded Q', and 'tuned amplifier tank'.
